questions.question: What does `[10, 9, 1, 100].sort()` return in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared, so '10' and '100' come before '9'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numeric order.

questions.question: Which sort guarantees O(n log n) in the worst case and is stable, at the cost of O(n) extra space?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always does log n levels of O(n) merging and keeps equal elements in order if the merge prefers the left half on ties, but it needs an auxiliary array.

questions.question: How can counting sort run faster than the Ω(n log n) lower bound?
options: It is not a comparison sort; it uses key values directly as array indices
It only works on already sorted data
questions.explanation: The lower bound applies to comparison-based sorts. Counting sort counts occurrences of small integer keys, giving O(n + k).

questions.question: In the merge-intervals solution, why is Math.max(last[1], e) used instead of just e?
options: Because intervals must be sorted by end time
Because the current interval may lie entirely inside the last merged one, as with [1, 10] followed by [2, 3]
questions.explanation: If the current interval ends earlier than the merged one, using e would wrongly shrink the merged interval.
